# Jacek Karpiński: Key Achievements and Legacy
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a pioneering Polish computer engineer whose innovations placed him among the leading figures in computer science in Poland. Despite significant personal hardship during World War II, including serious injuries and active participation in the resistance, Karpiński completed his studies rapidly and entered the field of electronics and computer science. His notable projects include the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH) for weather forecasting, the AKAT-1—the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer— and one of the earliest perceptrons based on Frank Rosenblatt’s ideas. Karpiński designed and built the KAR-65, which was the fastest Polish computer of its time and demonstrated advanced asynchronous architecture.
Karpiński’s most ambitious project was the K-202, a highly innovative minicomputer constructed in the early 1970s, which featured modularity, memory segmentation with paging, and asynchronous operation using microchips such as the Intel 4004. Although technologically superior to competitors like DEC’s PDP-11 and CTL’s Modular One, the K-202 faced political and institutional obstacles in communist Poland, and only 30 units were produced. Later in life, Karpiński contributed as an advisor to government officials and attempted various business ventures. He was recognized with prestigious awards, including the Officer's and Commander's Crosses of Polonia Restituta. Controversies include his cooperation with the Służba Bezpieczeństwa for technological intelligence and debates around the implications and recognition of his engineering achievements. Karpiński remains a significant, sometimes disputed, figure in the history of Polish computing.
